source_text: Tamen (sicut supra diximus) doleamus necesse est, quod nulla civitas impune latura sit sanguinis nostri effusionem, sicut et sub Hilariano praeside, cum de areis sepulturarum nostrarum acclamassent: Areae non sint; areae ipsorum non fuerunt. Messes enim suas non egerunt. Caeterum et imbre anni praeteriti quid commeruerit genus humanum apparuit, cataclysmum scilicet et retro fuisse propter incredulitates et iniquitates hominum; et ignes qui super moenia Carthaginis proxime pependerunt per noctem, quid minati sint, sciunt qui viderunt; et pristina tonitrua quid sonaverunt, sciunt qui obduruerunt. Omnia haec signa sunt imminentis irae Dei, quam necesse est, quoquo modo possumus, ut et annuntiemus, et praedicemus, et deprecemur interim localem esse: universalem enim et supremam suo tempore sentient, qui exempla ejus aliter interpretantur. Nam et sol ille in conventu Uticensi, extincto pene lumine, adeo portentum fuit, ut non potuerit ex ordinario deliquio hoc pati, positus in suo hypsomate et domicilio. Habetis astrologos. Possumus aeque et exitus quorumdam praesidum tibi proponere, qui in fine vitae suae recordati sunt deliquisse, quod vexassent chritianos. Vigellius Saturninus qui primus hic gladiumin nos egit, lumina amisit. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, cum indigne ferens uxorem suam ad hanc sectam transisse, christianos crudeliter tractasset, solusque in praetorio suo vastatus peste, cum vivus vermibus ebullisset: Nemo sciat, aiebat, ne gaudeant christiani. Postea cognito errore suo, quod tormentis quosdam a proposito suo excidere fecisset, pene christianus decessit. Caecilius Capella in illo exitu bysantino: Christiani gaudete, exclamavit. Sed et qui videntur sibi impune tulisse, venient in diem divini judicii. Tibi quoque optamus admonitionem solam fuisse, quod cum Adrimeticum Mavilum ad bestias damnasses, et statim haec vexatio subsecuta est, et nunc ex eadem caussa interpellatio sanguinis. Sed memento de caetero.

choices.english: Let there be no burial grounds

pass_b_english: Still, we have to grieve, because no state will escape punishment for shedding our blood—just as under the governor Hilarian, when they shouted from our burial grounds, 'No more burial grounds!' their own burial grounds vanished; they did not reap their own harvests. Meanwhile, what last year's rain brought the human race is plain: the flood, and the fact that it once came because of human unbelief and injustice. And the fires that recently hung over Carthage's walls at night—those who saw them know what they threatened. The former thunderclaps—those who hardened themselves know what they proclaimed. All these are signs of God's impending wrath, which we must, however we can, announce and preach and pray stays local for now; the universal and supreme wrath will come in its own time for those who interpret his signs otherwise. Even the sun at the assembly of Utica, its light nearly extinguished, was such a portent that it could not be an ordinary eclipse, fixed as it was in its own height and dwelling. You have your astrologers. We can just as well cite the ends of certain governors who, at the end of their lives, remembered they had sinned by persecuting Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, who first drew the sword against us here, lost his eyes. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, resenting that his wife had converted to this sect and treating Christians cruelly, was alone laid waste by pestilence in his own palace, boiling alive with worms. 'Let no one know,' he said, 'or the Christians will rejoice.' Later, recognizing his error in having forced some from their faith through torture, he died almost a Christian. Caecilius Capella, in that Byzantine crisis, cried out, 'Christians, rejoice!' But even those who think they have escaped unpunished will face the day of divine judgment. We also wish for you that the warning alone was enough: when you condemned Adrian and Mavilus to the beasts, this affliction followed immediately, and now the bloodshed has stopped for the same reason. But remember, for the future.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that preserves all nuances, including the specific cries of the historical figures and the theological distinctions regarding the local vs. universal wrath. The translation of 'Areae non sint; areae ipsorum non fuerunt' is handled well in Pass B as 'No more burial grounds!' their own burial grounds vanished, capturing the sense of the Latin. The translation of 'interpellatio sanguinis' as 'the bloodshed has stopped' in Pass B is a valid interpretation of the context of 'interpellatio' (interruption/calling to account) in relation to the previous 'vexatio'.
